analysis.one_liner: Forces major airlines to auction off some airport landing slots to new low-fare competitors.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At four congested East and Midwest airports, landing and takeoff rights ("slots") are limited and mostly held by the big established airlines. The bill would require the Transportation Department to take back up to 10% of those slots from major carriers and auction them only to new entrant and small carriers, with proceeds going to the federal airport trust fund. It would also open more long-distance routes out of Washington National Airport and require quick answers to airline complaints about predatory behavior.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers in markets dominated by one or two carriers, who studies cited in the bill show pay higher fares where competition is thin [S3]. Communities served by small and medium airports would get priority for new service [S2]. New entrant and low-fare carriers would gain access to slots they could not otherwise obtain [S2, S3].

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary must withdraw up to 10% of auctionable slots from major carriers at each slot-controlled airport for the first auction, and up to 5% for later ones, and auction them to new entrant or limited incumbent carriers only [S2, S3].
Applications proposing service to small and medium hub airports with no existing link to the slot-controlled airport get priority, directing new competition toward underserved communities [S2, S3].
Auction proceeds go to the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, recovering for the public part of the value of slots the government gave major carriers for free in 1985 [S2, S3].

The Secretary must grant perimeter-rule exemptions allowing carriers to fly longer routes out of Washington National if that increases competition in multiple markets, and must respond to predatory-behavior complaints within 90 days [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Major incumbent airlines, which would give up a share of slots they have held since the government assigned them in 1985, and which would face faster federal review of complaints that they use low fares to drive competitors out of a market [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: Auctioning slots adds a cost to access that did not exist when slots were assigned free, a cost carriers could pass into fares; the bill itself requires the Secretary not to base slot decisions on the expectation of federal revenue, acknowledging the tension [S3].
The bill directs the Secretary to limit commuter air carriers' use of air carrier slots, which could reduce feeder service that links small communities to major airports [S2, S3].

Perimeter-rule exemptions at Washington National would open long-haul routes from an airport whose neighbors and nearby communities rely on its existing noise, traffic, and local-service limits; the bill manages this with hourly-operation caps, Stage 3 aircraft-only rules, and congressional certification rather than eliminating the concerns [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest in scale: only a slice of slots at four airports is touched, and slots a carrier bought or exchanged for value are exempt. The upside — more competition and lower fares in concentrated markets, with a priority for underserved communities — is likely larger than the downside, though auction costs, reduced commuter slot use, and National Airport noise and congestion questions are legitimate costs the bill only partially addresses.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. McCain introduced the bill on October 29, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1, S5].
The full action history shows no further action after the committee referral; the bill died there when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major incumbent airlines that hold most of the slots at the four slot-controlled airports kept them intact — slots the bill's findings note they received largely free of charge in 1985. Travelers in markets dominated by those carriers saw no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big incumbent airlines holding the slots

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks arguing that slot controls block airline competition and raise fares, citing GAO findings on industry concentration [S1, S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or report appear in the action history [S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support and opposition was never tested.

industries.industry: Major incumbent airlines holding slots at high-density airports
industries.note: The bill would withdraw up to 10% of their auctionable slots for auction to competitors and subject them to 90-day federal responses to predatory-pricing complaints. Their slots are valuable assets granted largely free by the government in 1985, so blocking the bill preserved that position.

They alone could bid in slot auctions and get dedicated allocations, giving them access to airports they could not otherwise enter. Expanding their presence is the mechanism by which fares fall for travelers.

The bill directs the Secretary to limit commuter carriers' use of air carrier slots, weighing that use against slots for other carriers. Smaller communities connected by commuter service could feel this.
